actions.text: Welcome, everyone. Over the next hour we're going to take apart one of the cleanest relative-value trades on the volatility desk — dispersion. By the end of the session you'll be able to quote it, size it, decompose its P and L, and be honest about what actually kills it. Let's start with the whole thing in one line.
The title of this page is the thesis of the entire lesson. If you only remember one sentence from today, make it this one — everything else is just the plumbing that supports it.

You are trading correlation, not direction. You have no view on whether the index goes up or down — your view is on how tightly the members move together. Correlation is the one number that ties index vol to the vol of its constituents, and that is precisely why it is quotable, hedgeable, and tradable as an asset class in its own right.

Here is the book. You are short index vega and long single-name vega. Mechanically you sell straddles or variance on the index, and you buy the same on the constituents, sized so the notionals line up. The legs almost cancel in outright volatility terms — that is the whole point.

Which brings us to the net risk. Your outright vol exposure is roughly flat — you are not long or short vol in the aggregate. What is left over is a long correlation position. You make money when realized correlation comes in below what you paid for it, and you lose when the names start moving together.

So the real bet, stated cleanly, is the gap between implied and realized correlation. Not the level of the market, not the direction of the index — just that spread. Carry on this trade is the premium you collect for being short that gap; the tail is what you pay when the gap blows out against you.

Here is the roadmap from the quote to the tail. First, extracting implied correlation from the index and its names. Second, the P and L identity — vega times the correlation spread. Third, the construction choice: which names, and at what weights. And fourth, the tail, the scenario that ultimately pays for all that carry. Let's take them one at a time.

actions.text: We just walked through the four pillars of the trade. Now let's put a number on the second one, because the whole dispersion trade is ultimately a position in a single quantity: correlation.
There are two ways the market quotes that number, and they don't always agree. The first is realized correlation — the backward-looking one.

Realized correlation is just the rolling average of the pairwise correlations among the index members, computed from returns and nothing else. It needs a window, it needs history, and by the time you can measure it, it's already happened.
The second is implied correlation — the forward-looking quote. This is the one you actually trade.

And here's the elegance of it: implied correlation is solved backwards out of option prices. No returns required. All you need is the index vol surface and the single-name surfaces, and the market hands you a correlation quote.

So how do we extract it? Start with the index variance identity. The implied index variance equals rho implied times the average member variance, plus one minus rho implied, times that same average member variance divided by N. Everything here comes straight off the vol surfaces.

And because the implied index variance and the average member variance are both observable, we can solve for rho directly. That makes implied correlation a live quote — it re-marks with every tick of the surface, not once a day like the realized number.

Now watch what happens as N gets large. For a big index like the Nikkei 225 or the S&P 500, that one-over-N term collapses toward zero, and the whole relationship reduces to something you can carry in your head: rho implied is approximately the implied index variance divided by the average member variance. One number, two quotes — and a spread between them that we can trade.

actions.text: We've got the two quotes from the last page. Now let's actually run the extraction on a real index. NK225 — the Nikkei 225 — is a clean lab: two hundred and twenty-five names, a deep liquid index option market, and a listed vol surface on every single member. That last part is what makes the drill possible, because we need member implied vols to strip the variances out of the index.

The drill itself is one line. Implied correlation is approximately the index implied variance divided by the average member implied variance. Index implied vol is twenty-nine percent, so squared, that's about 0.084. Members are averaging roughly forty percent implied vol, so an average variance of 0.16. Divide 0.084 by 0.16, and implied correlation comes out at roughly 0.52.

Now the reality check. Realized pairwise correlation across those members is 0.50 — measured from actual returns, not implied from anything. So on day one: implied 0.52 against realized 0.50. Two points of richness. It's real, but it isn't yet a business.

Watch what happens as the index re-prices. Run the same extraction at thirty, thirty-one, thirty-two and thirty-five percent index vol, and implied correlation climbs: 0.52, 0.56, 0.60, 0.64, and 0.77 at the top. Member variances barely moved — all of that lift is coming from the index. At thirty-two percent, implied correlation is 0.64 against that same realized 0.50. A fourteen point gap. That's no longer a vol view.

And that's the whole point: the trade is the gap, not the level. Implied correlation rich to realized means you sell correlation — short the index's implied linkage, long dispersion, collecting the spread for doing it. But note the sensitivity. One point of index implied vol moves implied correlation by roughly 0.04. You can't take the correlation view without carrying that vega with it. The surface is the position. Next, let's build the explorer and see how this gap behaves across strikes, tenors, and vol regimes — before we size anything.

questions.analysis: For equal weights and equal member vols: index variance = sigma_index^2 = member_vol^2 * [1/N + ((N-1)/N) * rho_impl]. Rearranging gives rho_impl = (N * (sigma_index/member_vol)^2 - 1) / (N - 1). Plug in: N = 225, sigma_index = 0.32, member_vol = 0.40. Ratio = (0.32/0.40)^2 = 0.64. So rho_impl = (225 * 0.64 - 1) / 224 = (144 - 1) / 224 = 143/224 = 0.6384, or approximately 64%. Options B, C, and D do not match the implied correlation extracted from the index-member vol relationship.

actions.text: Checkpoint is behind us. Now let's open up the book itself — the two legs that make up the dispersion position, and the dollars-per-vega identity that tells us what this thing actually pays for.

The short leg is index vol. One liquid line — the listed index option — and we are selling vega there. That is the leg everyone can trade, it is the leg that prices cleanly, and it is the leg carrying the implied correlation we are short.

The long leg is the single names, the constituents themselves. We buy vega back across the basket and we size that ratio so the whole book lands close to vega-neutral. Close to neutral, not exactly neutral — that residual is the entire point of the trade.

Here is the identity that governs everything. P and L divided by V — that is your profit per unit of vega — equals the average realized vol of the members minus their average implied vol, and then minus that same difference for the index. Read it as: what the names actually realize versus what we paid for them, netted against what the index realizes versus what we sold. Every dollar of this book flows through those two brackets.

Breakeven falls straight out of that. If the members realize exactly at implied, the first bracket is zero, and the index difference is zero as well — which is precisely the statement that realized correlation equals implied correlation. Realize below implied, the book wins. Realize above, the book loses, and it loses on the whole vega notional, not on some delta slice. And notice what is absent from the identity: direction. There is no delta term anywhere in it. This position is a pure correlation exposure, which is exactly why hedging the index beta is a separate problem we have to solve on top of the trade. Next, we decompose this P and L line by line and see where each dollar actually comes from.

actions.text: Okay, so we've got the gap identified and we know it's real. Now the honest question: where does the money actually come from on this book? Let's decompose the P and L, line by line, and stop telling ourselves it's a carry trade.

Start with the carry term. Theta over vega — the theta you pay for every unit of vega you're long. On this book that ratio is slightly negative. The long members bleed roughly sigma over two T, and because the book's average sigma sits above index sigma, that bleed is a touch worse than a naive sizing would suggest. So carry is not our friend here. It's a cost.

And here's the asymmetry that makes it worse. Average sigma — the book's implied — is greater than index sigma. The long legs carry more vol per unit of vega, which means they also carry more theta decay per unit of vega. You are paying more rent on the long side than the index leg is earning back.

So if carry is negative, what's the engine? Realized dispersion — full stop. The positive expectancy does not come from carry. It comes from realized correlation printing below implied correlation. Theta is simply the fee you pay for the right to be short correlation. Frame it that way and the trade stops looking like a yield play and starts looking like a long-vol-of-dispersion position.
Quick notation check before we read the table: sigma real is realized vol, sigma avg is the book's implied. Everything below is measured per unit of vega.
Here's the component breakdown. We're separating theta cost, the member realized-vol term, the index realized-vol term, and then net P and L — each with its sign and its magnitude per unit vega.

Look at where the weight sits. The theta line is small and negative — the drag we've been talking about. The member realized-vol term is where the edge lives, and the index realized-vol term is what you're short. Net P and L is dominated by that dispersion spread, not by the carry. That's the key takeaway: the trade earns from realized dispersion, and theta is the admission price. Next, we look at why you can't flatten vega and gamma at the same time.

data.title: You Can't Flatten Vega and Gamma at Once

actions.text: We closed the last page on theta being the admission price. Now here is the structural problem underneath it: you cannot flatten vega and gamma at the same time. On this page we work out why, and more importantly, which residual each construction choice leaves you holding.

Start with the identity. Vega divided by dollar gamma equals sigma times time to expiry. The spot level cancels entirely — it sits in the numerator and the denominator, so it drops out. Read it the other way and it is just as clean: dollar gamma per unit of vega is one over sigma times T. So per gamma-dollar, vega scales with sigma times T, and nothing else.

That has an immediate consequence for the basket. Look at the low-vol leg — the index. Its implied vol is the lowest in the structure, so it is the leg that carries the most dollar gamma per unit of vega. Cheap vol buys you more gamma per unit of vega risk, and that asymmetry is what makes the configuration choice bite.

Here is the menu. Vega-flat leaves a residual short dollar gamma, which is exactly what you would expect — the correlation-pure book has vol-level exposure of roughly zero. Gamma-flat on dollar gamma, which is our desk convention, forces you to over-buy name vega, so the residual is long vega: you gain on vol rallies and you pay theta for the privilege. Gamma-flat per contract, plain lot matching, leaves you short vega instead: you receive theta, and you give it back on a vol rally.

None of these three is wrong. The residual is the configuration choice, not an error — and that is the whole message of this page. So pick the residual you are actually paid to carry. If your mandate is long vol, go dollar-gamma-flat and wear the long vega. If the mandate is carry, lot-match and accept the short vega. What is not defensible is running one of these without knowing which one you are in.

data.title: When the Trade Loses: The Tail

actions.text: Now let's flip the trade over and look at what happens when it goes against us. Same book, same construction — but this is the week you do not want to be living through. This is the tail.

Here's the stress week. Realized correlation across the members jumps from about zero point five zero up to zero point seven five, while each member is realizing forty percent vol. And notice, nothing has to go wrong in any single name — the members can trade exactly where they have been trading. What changes is the relationship between them.

So let's reprice the index leg with those inputs. The fair index variance is rho times member variance, plus one minus rho times member variance divided by N. The first term is the pure correlation effect, the second is whatever diversification is left over — and in a wide basket that second term is small.
That symbol on the slide is our target — the fair index variance. Feed the stressed inputs into it and watch how much of the answer is driven by correlation alone.
Plug the numbers in. Zero point seven five times zero point one six gives zero point one two. Take the square root of that, and the fair index vol is roughly thirty four point six percent.

Now compare that to what you actually sold. You're short the index leg at thirty two implied. Fair is thirty four point six. That is roughly two point six vol points of mark-to-market loss on a leg where you are short vega — and every further point of correlation prints another tick into that number.
The slide lays out the losing conditions. Correlation spikes, realized dispersion collapses, and the index realizes far above its implied.

And here is the part that matters for your book: those are not three separate risks you can hedge one at a time. They are all the same event. When correlation spots, dispersion collapses by construction, and the index realization overshoots. Your long dispersion leg and your short index leg do not offset — the loss is non-linear and it is path-dependent.

Which brings us straight back to the premium we discussed earlier. The correlation risk premium is the compensation for eating exactly this tail. You are short insurance that the market systematically overprices — and this is the week the market comes to collect on it.

actions.text: And that tail is precisely why we spent this session building the trade piece by piece. Let's pull the machinery together now — here on the review page — into a short set of rules you can actually act on at the desk.

Rule one: two quotes, one number. Correlation is never quoted outright on any screen. You extract implied correlation from the index implied vol against the single-name implied vols, and you measure realized correlation from the returns themselves. Two different quotes, blended into one number — and the entire trade lives in the gap between them.

Rule two: the premium. When implied correlation sits above realized, you're being paid to be short correlation. Practically, that means sell correlation, buy dispersion — short index vol, long the names. That spread is your carry, and it's the compensation for taking the other side of a systematically overpriced hedge.

Rule three: know what actually drives your P and L. It's the correlation gap, not direction — direction gets hedged out, so what's left is the gap between implied and realized. Theta is a small cost, a drag you carry, while realized dispersion is the engine. The wider realized dispersion comes in relative to what you paid for it, the more of that premium you keep.

Rule four: respect the tail. In stress, correlation doesn't drift — it spikes. Everything goes to one and the short index vol leg is what hurts. That's the scenario we just walked through, and it's exactly what the premium is paying you for. You are short insurance the market overprices, and you get paid for holding that risk, not for pretending it isn't there.

And rule five, where we go next: sizing the legs, vega ratioing so the book is neutral to a parallel vol move, gamma asymmetry, and why single-name skew matters so much when you're the one buying it. That's the construction detail that separates a good idea from a position that actually survives a week like the one we just described. Keep these five rules in front of you — the assessment on the next page leans directly on them.

elements.content: Review & Key Takeaways

Two Quotes, One Number

Implied corr from index vs single-name vols; realized from returns.

The Premium

Implied > realized: sell corr, buy dispersion — short index vol, long names.

P&L Driver

Correlation gap, not direction. Theta is a cost; dispersion is the engine.

The Tail

Stress brings a correlation spike — that is what the premium pays you for.
Next: sizing the legs, vega ratioing, gamma asymmetry, single-name skew when buying.

actions.text: Alright, the final assessment. Four questions, and they pull together the whole arc of what we just covered — reading the gap out of two quotes, the anatomy of the book, the P&L decomposition, and where the tail does its damage. Take each one on your own and take your time; there's no clock running on you.

Answer them independently — that's the only way the result tells you anything useful. Hit submit when you're done, and I'll sit down with you right after to walk through every one of them, especially the ones that gave you trouble. Go ahead and get started.
